title: Welcome and Table of Contents
summary: What SS2 English Language First Term is about, how to use the notes, and a map of every unit.

p: In SS2 you move from simple correctness to skilful, mature English. This term you learn grammar (nominalisation, noun phrases, pronouns, plurals, adverbs), oral English (consonants, clusters, transcription and stress), writing (expository and argumentative essays and a scientific report), reading skills (summary, main ideas, note-taking and listening) and rich vocabulary.

Study one unit at a time. Do the practice work in your notebook before you check the answers. At the end of every unit are practice questions. They do not count towards a mark; they help you check that you understood. Answer them all correctly to complete the unit.

title: Grammar: Nominalisation of Adjectives and Verbs
summary: How verbs and adjectives are turned into nouns by adding suffixes or by conversion, and why this makes writing formal.

p: Nominalisation is turning another part of speech, mostly a verb or an adjective, into a noun or noun phrase. It moves your writing from simple actions and qualities to ideas and things. It is a mark of formal, academic and professional writing.
Without nominalisation: 'The manager decided quickly. This was efficient.' With nominalisation: 'The manager's quick decision showed efficiency.'
This is the commonest way. Notice that the spelling often changes.

head: Suffix
Verb to noun
Adjective to noun
rows: act → action; decide → decision; expand → expansion
govern → government; pay → payment; argue → argument
arrive → arrival; refuse → refusal; dismiss → dismissal
stupid → stupidity; pure → purity; cruel → cruelty
happy → happiness; good → goodness; kind → kindness
grow → growth; die → death; bear → birth
strong → strength; wide → width; long → length
marry → marriage; break → breakage; use → usage

p: The word keeps the same form but works as a noun. 'His daily run keeps him fit.' 'There was a big fight after the match.' 'I need a good rest.' 'She has a great love for music.'
'The company invested heavily in research, which caused it to innovate rapidly' becomes 'The company's heavy investment in research led to rapid innovation.'
'The patient was anxious, and this was evident to the doctor' becomes 'The patient's anxiety was evident to the doctor.'
'If we collaborate effectively, we will succeed' becomes 'Effective collaboration will lead to success.'

activity: Turn into nouns: amaze, solve, develop, dark, accurate, young. Rewrite: 'The employees argued fiercely, which disrupted the meeting.' (amazement; solution; development; darkness; accuracy; youth. The employees' fierce argument disrupted the meeting.)

title: Oral English: Voiced and Voiceless Consonants
summary: What voicing means, how to test for it, and the pairs of consonants that differ only in voicing.

p: Consonant sounds differ in whether the vocal cords vibrate. In a voiceless sound the vocal cords are apart and do not vibrate; only air passes. In a voiced sound the vocal cords are close and vibrate, giving a buzzing feeling in the throat.
Test: put your fingers on your throat. Say 'ssssss' (like a snake): nothing. Say 'zzzzzz' (like a bee): you feel a buzz. So /s/ is voiceless and /z/ is voiced.
Many consonants form pairs with exactly the same mouth position; only voicing differs.
Your lesson note gives 'chin / jin' as a pair. 'Jin' is not a normal word, so use 'chin / gin' or 'cheap / jeep'. The words 'thin' and 'thy' in the original table are also fine as /θ/ and /ð/.

activity: In each pair, which word has the voiced sound? (a) fan / van; (b) price / prize; (c) batch / badge. (van; prize; badge.) Write five minimal pairs of your own, such as rope / robe.

title: Summary Writing: Features and Rules
summary: What a summary is, the features of a good summary, a list of do's and don'ts and a worked example.

p: A summary is a short, objective and fluent statement of the main ideas of a text, written in your own words. It shows that you understand the passage by taking away examples, extra details and repetition and keeping only the central message. It is not a comment on the text or a criticism of it.

Brevity: much shorter than the original. Clarity: easy to understand and correct in grammar. Objectivity: only the author's ideas, not yours. Completeness: all the main points that answer the question. Paraphrasing: mostly in your own words.
Study the table.

head: Do
Do not
rows: Read the question carefully and find what it asks
Start writing before you understand the passage
Underline topic sentences and key ideas
Include your own opinions or examples
Paraphrase using synonyms and new sentence patterns
Use connectives such as furthermore, consequently, however
Use figures of speech, rhetorical questions or minor details
Keep to the word or sentence limit
Change or distort the author's meaning

p: Passage: 'In contemporary society, the spread of digital technology has had a deep effect on social life. Many experts say that while technology links people over great distances, it can also weaken face-to-face communication. For instance, constant use of smartphones in company can lead to "phubbing", ignoring one's companions in favour of a phone. This can cause feelings of neglect and reduce the depth of personal bonds. So it is important to find a healthy balance between digital and real-world contact.'

Question: in one sentence, state the negative effect of digital technology on social life. Steps: find the key words in the question (negative effect, digital technology, social interaction); find the matching points in the passage (weakens face-to-face talk, phubbing, neglect, shallow bonds); put them in your own words.
Answer: 'Digital technology can weaken face-to-face communication by encouraging habits such as phubbing, which damage the quality of personal relationships.'

title: Oral English: Consonant Clusters
summary: What consonant clusters are, two-, three- and four-consonant clusters at the start and end of words, and the error of epenthesis.

p: A consonant cluster is a group of two or more consonant sounds together in one syllable with no vowel sound between them. Saying them well makes your English clear and natural. A common mistake is epenthesis, adding a vowel (usually the schwa /ə/) inside a cluster. Correct: film /fɪlm/. Wrong: 'fi-lim'. Another example: 'school' pronounced 'sukool'.

Initial (at the start): /s/ plus consonant (stay, sky, slow, swim, snow); /l/ blends (blow, clean, fly, glass, play); /r/ blends (bring, cry, dry, free, grow, pray, tree). Final (at the end): -st (last, past, test), -nd (hand, send, find), -sk (task, desk, ask), -mp (jump, lamp, camp), -ft (left, gift, soft), -ld (gold, hold, child).

Initial clusters nearly always begin with /s/: /spr/ (spring, spray, sprout), /str/ (street, strong, strike), /skr/ (script, scream, scrub), /spl/ (splash, split, spleen). Final clusters often come from adding -s or -ed: -nts (tents, wants), -mps (jumps, lamps), -sks (tasks, desks), -pts (scripts, adapts), -lps (helps, gulps).

These are usually at the end of words. Say each consonant cleanly and quickly without inserting a vowel: twelfths /twɛlfθs/, fifths, strengths /strɛŋθs/, lengths, texts /tɛksts/, next /nɛkst/, glimpsed /ɡlɪmpst/, prompts /prɒmpts/, attempts.

activity: Say five times: 'The strong sprinter glimpsed the scrambled scripts on the desks.' How many consonants are in the final cluster of 'glimpsed'? (Four: /mpst/.) Which has a four-consonant cluster: thanks, prompts, lists? (prompts.)

title: Writing: the Expository Essay
summary: The purpose and structure of an expository essay: introduction with hook and thesis, three body paragraphs with topic sentences, and a conclusion; with a worked outline.

p: An expository essay explains, describes or informs. Its aim is a balanced, factual explanation. Unlike an argumentative essay, it does not try to persuade the reader to share an opinion. It 'exposes' information clearly and logically. The tone is objective.
Think of a house: the introduction is the foundation, the body paragraphs are the walls and the conclusion is the roof.

Introduction (one paragraph): a hook (a striking fact, a question or a statement to catch interest); background (short context or definitions); the thesis statement (one clear sentence stating the main point).

Body (usually three paragraphs): each paragraph develops one main point that supports the thesis. It begins with a topic sentence and continues with supporting details (facts, statistics, examples, explanations), with an optional concluding sentence. Use transitions such as furthermore, moreover, in addition, consequently and for instance.
Conclusion (one paragraph): restate the thesis in new words; summarise the main points; end with a final thought or recommendation. Do not bring in new ideas.

Topic: 'The three major causes of road accidents in Nigeria'. Thesis: 'The high rate of road accidents in Nigeria is chiefly caused by human error, poor vehicle maintenance and inadequate road infrastructure.'

Body 1: human error (speeding, dangerous overtaking, driving under the influence, using the phone). Body 2: poor condition of vehicles (bald tyres, faulty brakes, broken lights, weak inspection). Body 3: bad roads (potholes, no signs, dead streetlights, eroded roads). Conclusion: accidents come from driver behaviour, vehicle condition and road quality, so stricter law enforcement, public education and investment in roads are needed.

activity: Write a 400-word expository essay on 'The roles and responsibilities of a good citizen' or 'The main causes and effects of the erosion of cultural values in your community'. Write a thesis for: 'The benefits of a digital literacy programme in secondary schools.'

title: Structure: Nouns and Noun Phrases
summary: Types of nouns, the parts of a noun phrase, the five functions of a noun phrase and the difference between a noun phrase and a noun clause.

p: Proper: names (Chinua, Abuja, Christmas). Common: general names (artist, city). Abstract: ideas and qualities (freedom, bravery, justice). Collective: groups (team, flock, fleet). Concrete: things the senses can perceive (rain, sand, perfume). Countable: have plurals (book, books; child, children). Uncountable: no plural (advice, furniture, information).

A noun phrase is a group of words built round a noun (the headword) which works as one unit. Structure: (determiner) + (pre-modifiers) + headword + (post-modifiers). Determiners: a, an, the, this, my, some, five. Pre-modifiers: adjectives or other nouns ('university student'). Post-modifiers: prepositional phrases, relative clauses, participle phrases.
Examples: 'a brilliant idea' (determiner, pre-modifier, headword); 'a brilliant idea for a new project' (adds a post-modifier); 'the tall, intelligent boy who won the prize'.

Subject (S): [The diligent student] passed the exam. Object (O): He bought [a new bicycle]. Subject complement (C): Mr Bello is [a dedicated teacher]. Object complement (C): They elected him [their chairman]. Object of a preposition (OP): She put the book on [the wooden table].

A noun phrase has no subject and verb of its own: 'I know [the correct answer to the question].' A noun clause has its own subject and verb and works as a noun. It is introduced by words such as that, what, why, how, whether, whoever: 'I know [what you did last summer].' '[Why he resigned] remains a mystery' (the clause is the subject). 'The truth is [that she never arrived]' (the clause is the subject complement).

activity: Identify the noun phrase and its function: 'He painted the old garden fence.' (the old garden fence: object.) 'Her greatest ambition is to become a surgeon.' (Her greatest ambition: subject; a surgeon: subject complement of the infinitive.) Is it a noun phrase or clause: 'I understand what you mean'? (noun clause.)

title: Oral English: Transcription and Stress Marking
summary: The International Phonetic Alphabet, pure vowels and diphthongs, and basic rules for marking word stress.

p: Transcription is writing speech sounds with the symbols of the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA), so pronunciation can be recorded exactly, whatever the spelling. Word stress is extra force on one syllable, making it louder, longer and higher in pitch. Correct stress is often more important for being understood than perfect individual sounds.

Pure vowels (monophthongs): /iː/ see, beat; /ɪ/ sit, bin; /e/ bed, pen; /æ/ cat, bad; /ɑː/ car, father; /ɒ/ hot, clock; /ɔː/ saw, born; /ʊ/ put, book; /uː/ too, food; /ʌ/ cup, luck; /ɜː/ bird, fern; /ə/ about, sister (the schwa, the most common vowel sound).
Diphthongs (gliding vowels): /eɪ/ day, make; /aɪ/ my, time; /ɔɪ/ boy, coin; /aʊ/ now, house; /əʊ/ go, home; /ɪə/ here, beard; /eə/ hair, care; /ʊə/ pure, tour.

The stress mark (ˈ) is put before the stressed syllable. One-syllable words carry the stress (dog, run). Two-syllable nouns and adjectives usually take stress on the first syllable (PRESent, HAPpy); two-syllable verbs usually on the second (preSENT, deCIDE, beGIN). In longer words the suffix often decides: stress the syllable before -tion, -sion, -ic, -ity, -graphy (eduCAtion, ecoNOmic, aBILity, phoTOgraphy); stress falls on -ee and -eer (employEE, engiNEER).
photograph /ˈfəʊtəɡrɑːf/ (first syllable); photographer /fəˈtɒɡrəfə/ (second syllable, because of -grapher); photographic /ˌfəʊtəˈɡræfɪk/ (third syllable, before -ic).
